Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 1:

﴿Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾. On this there are three opinions. The first: do not speak on a matter before he (ﷺ) speaks on it, and do not decide on a matter except by his judgment. The second: do not put the rulers forward in his presence, for he is the one who appoints whom he wishes. The third: do not walk ahead of him when he walks. This applies only according to the reading of Ya'qub, "lā tuqaddimū" with a fatha on the tā', the qāf and the dāl. The first opinion is the most apparent, because it is the habit of the Arabs to share in opinion and for each person to speak whatever occurs to him, so some people may have done this in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah forbade them from it. For this reason Mujahid said: its meaning is, do not act presumptuously toward Allah in anything until He mentions it through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ). He said "before Allah" only because the Prophet (ﷺ) speaks only by revelation from Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 2:

﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ Allah commanded the believers to observe this etiquette with the Prophet (ﷺ), as an honour to him and a glorification of him. The reason for it was that some coarse Bedouin Arabs used to raise their voices. ﴿Lest your deeds should be nullified﴾ is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose, an accusative of cause), its implied sense being: out of fear that your deeds would be nullified if you raise your voices above his, or speak loudly to him (ﷺ). So the maf'ul li-ajlihi is linked to both verbs together in terms of meaning. As for its grammatical linkage (i'rab), according to the Basrans it is linked to the second verb, which is ﴿and do not speak loudly﴾, while according to the Kufans it is linked to the first, which is ﴿Do not raise your voices﴾. This nullification occurs because lack of etiquette towards him (ﷺ) and falling short in honouring him nullify good deeds, even if a believer does them, due to the gravity of what he has fallen into of that. It has been said: the verse is addressed to the hypocrites, but this is weak, because of its opening words: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ and its saying: ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, for it is not valid to say this to a hypocrite, since he does it deliberately "out of audacity" while intending it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah﴾ It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. When the preceding verse was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I will not speak to you except in a whisper." Umar would lower his speech when the Prophet ﷺ asked him something. Yet its wording remains general in application. The meaning of ﴿امتحن﴾ (imtahana, "tested"): he tested it and found it as it should be, just as gold is tested by fire, so that it is found pure. It is also said its meaning is: he trained it for piety until it became strong enough to bear it without strain. And it is said: its meaning is that Allah purified it for piety.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers—most of them do not use their reason.﴾

Al-Hujurat (the private chambers): the plural of hujrah, a piece of land enclosed by a wall. Each of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ had a chamber of her own. The verse was revealed concerning the delegation of Banu Tamim. They came to the Prophet ﷺ, entered the mosque, drew near the chambers of the Prophet's wives, stopped outside them, and called out: "O Muhammad, come out to us!" Their doing so showed rudeness, crudeness of manners and lack of respect. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ waited for a while and then came out to them. One of them, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, said to him: "O Muhammad, my praise is an adornment and my blame is a disgrace." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Woe to you, that is Allah, the Exalted."

﴿most of them do not use their reason﴾: This may bear two meanings. The first is that among them there are a few who do use their reason, and the negation of reason is applied to most of them, not to all of them. The second is that all of them are among those who do not use their reason, and the word "most" (akthar) is used in place of a total negation. The first is more apparent in the wording of the text, and the second is more eloquent in censure.

ﷺ here is rendered as (ﷺ) per instructions.

"Had they been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them." That is, better in reward, and in the Prophet's (ﷺ) being at ease, his fulfilling their needs, and his disapproval of their action being a discipline for them and a lesson for others.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 6:

﴿If a sinner brings you a report, then verify it﴾. Its occasion of revelation: the Prophet (ﷺ) sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the Banu al-Mustaliq to collect their zakat (obligatory alms). It is related that he had enmity toward them, so he intended to harm them. He turned back from part of his route and lied about them, saying to the Prophet (ﷺ): "They have withheld the charity from me, driven me away, and apostatized." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry and resolved to fight them, and he considered the matter. Then their delegation arrived, denying that. It is also related that when al-Walid ibn 'Uqba drew near them, they came out to meet him, welcoming him. He saw them from a distance, was frightened of them, and suspected evil from them, so he turned back and said what he said. It is also related that he was informed that they had said: "We will not give him charity, and we will not obey him," so he turned back and said what he said. Thus the sinner referred to in the verse is al-Walid ibn 'Uqba. He did not cease after that to commit the acts of sinners, until he led the people in the dawn prayer four rakahs while he was intoxicated, then said to them: "Shall I add more for you, if you wish?" Then this ruling remains in force for everyone who is characterized by this attribute until the end of time.

It was also read as ﹛fatabayyanu﹜ (from tabayyun, clarification), and as ﹛fatathabbatu﹜ with the letter thā' (from tathabbut, verification). This reading is strengthened by the fact that when it was revealed, it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Deliberation is from Allah, and haste is from Shaytan."

Those who hold that the single report (khabar al-wahid) is acceptable use this verse as evidence, because the implication of the address (dalil al-khitab) requires that the report of a non-sinner is acceptable. Al-Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Balluti said: This verse refutes those who say that all Muslims are upright (adl), because Allah commanded verification before acceptance, so the one whose condition is unknown is feared to be a sinner.

﴿Lest you harm a people in ignorance﴾: this is in the position of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi); its estimated sense is: out of fear that you harm a people in ignorance. The reference is to fighting the Banu al-Mustaliq, since al-Walid mentioned what he mentioned about them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 7:

﴿Had he obeyed you in much of the affair, you would have been in distress.﴾ Meaning: you would have been wretched. Al-ʿanat (distress, hardship) is hardship. He said "law yutiʿukum" (if he obeyed you) and did not say "law atāʿakum" (if he had obeyed you), to indicate that they were wanting the continuation of his obedience to them, peace and blessings be upon him, whereas the truth is otherwise. What is obligatory is that they obey him, not that he obey them. This is because the opinion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is better and more correct than the opinion of anyone else, and if he were to obey people in their opinions, they would be ruined. So what is obligatory for them is submission to him and returning to his command. The reference to this is in His words: ﴿But Allah has made faith beloved to you and has made it attractive in your hearts﴾, and the verse continues.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verses 9–10:

﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them.﴾ Scholars differed regarding the occasion of its revelation. The majority said: it refers to what occurred between the Muslims and those partisans among them who followed ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by him while he was heading to visit Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah during his illness, and the donkey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urinated. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The stench of your donkey has harmed me." ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah retorted, and the people quarreled until a fight broke out between the two groups, with blows exchanged with palm stalks. It is said: with iron weapons. It is also said: its cause was that two factions of the Ansar fought with each other, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reconciled them after great effort. Then its ruling remains in force until the end of time.

He said "iqtatalu" (they fought) and not "iqtatalā" (they two fought) because the ṭāʾifah (group) carries the sense of qawm (people) and nās (people), so it has the meaning of a plural.

﴿But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses.﴾ In this verse Allah commands fighting the transgressing group, and that is when it becomes clear that it is transgressing. As for the strife that occurs among the Muslims, the scholars differed over it in two opinions. The first is that it is not permissible to rise up in any of it or to fight, and this is the position of Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Dharr, and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. Their evidence is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Fighting a Muslim is disbelief." And his command, peace be upon him, to break swords in times of strife. The second opinion is that rising up in it is obligatory so that the transgressing group may be restrained. This is the view of ʿAli, ʿAʾishah, Talhah, al-Zubayr, and most of the Companions, and it is the position of Malik and others among the jurists. Their evidence is this verse.

If we follow the first opinion, then if someone enters upon a person who has withdrawn from both groups, into his home, intending his self or his property, he should repel him from himself, even if that leads to his being killed, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever is killed defending his self or his property is a martyr."

If we follow the second opinion, scholars differed about with whom one should rise up in times of strife. It was said: with the great majority (al-sawad al-aʿzam). It was said: with the scholars. It was said: with whoever believes the truth is with him. The ruling on fighting during strife is that one does not finish off the wounded, does not pursue the fleeing, does not kill a captive, and does not distribute the spoils of war. ﴿Until it returns﴾ meaning, returns to the truth.

﴿So make peace between your two brothers.﴾ He mentioned it in the dual form because the least number among whom transgression occurs is two. It was also said that by "the two brothers" he meant the Aws and the Khazraj. Ibn ʿAmir recited "bayna ikhwatikum" with the taʾ on the plural form, and it was also recited "bayna ikhwanikum" with the nun, likewise in the plural.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil, *al-Tashil li-'Ulum al-Tanzil*) on Surah 49, verse 11:**

﴿Let not a people ridicule another people, perhaps they may be better than them﴾. He forbade mockery, which is deriding people. ﴿Perhaps they may be better than them﴾, meaning that the one being mocked may be better than the mocker in the sight of God. This is the reason given for the prohibition. ﴿Nor let women ridicule other women﴾. Since "a people" applies only to men, he added women separately. ﴿And do not defame one another﴾, meaning that some of you should not revile others. Al-lamz (defamation) is finding fault, whether by speech, gesture, or otherwise. I will mention the difference between it and al-hamz in Surat al-Humazah. ﴿Yourselves﴾ here is in the same sense as His saying: ﴿So greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames﴾, meaning that no one should call another by a nickname. Al-tanabuz bil-alqab (insulting by nicknames) is calling someone by them. The muhaddithun (hadith scholars) permitted saying al-A'mash (the weak-sighted) and al-A'raj (the lame) and the like when necessity calls for it, provided that the intention is not to belittle or demean.

﴿Wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾. By "the name" he means that a person is called a sinner (fasiq) after having been called a believer. There are three interpretations of this. The first is the reprehensibility of combining defiance with faith, meaning that whoever does any of these forbidden things is a sinner, even if he is a believer. The second is that it is wretched for a man to say to another, "O sinner," after his faith, like the way some said to a Jew who had embraced Islam, "O Jew." The third is that the verse refers to one who has become a sinner while not being a believer, and this is according to the view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position between belief and disbelief).

﴿Avoid much suspicion﴾, meaning evil suspicion about the Muslims. As for good suspicion, it is laudable. ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin.﴾ It has been said that the sin here means lying, based on his saying ﷺ: "Suspicion is the most untrue of speech," because it may not correspond to reality. It has also been said that it is only a sin when one speaks it. If one does not speak it, one is excused, because a person cannot prevent passing thoughts. Some scholars used this verse as evidence for the validity of *sadd al-dharai'* (blocking the means, i.e., preventing things that lead to harm) in the Sharia, since He commanded avoiding much suspicion and informed that some of it is sin. Thus, by avoiding the majority, one guards against falling into the part that is sin. ﴿And do not spy﴾, meaning do not search for what people conceal. Al-Hasan recited *tahassasu* with the letter ḥā' and *tajassus* with the letter jīm. *Tajassus* (searching out hidden faults) is used for evil, and *tahassus* with ḥā' for good. It has also been said that *tajassus* is what is done from behind, while *tahassus* with ḥā' means entering and seeking information. ﴿And let not some of you backbite others.﴾ The meaning is: let none of you mention about his Muslim brother what he would dislike if he heard it. *Ghība* (backbiting) is mentioning a person with what he dislikes regarding his character, his physical form, his religion, his actions, or anything else. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Backbiting is that you mention your believing brother with what he dislikes." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if it is true?" He said: "If you say what is false, that is slander (*buhtān*)." Backbiting has been permitted in several situations, among them: criticizing a witness, a narrator, or a marriage partner and similar matters, and warning against people of misguidance.

﴿Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it.﴾ Nafi' recited *maytan* with a tashdīd (*mayyitan*). Allah likened backbiting to eating the flesh of a human being who is dead, and the Arabs liken backbiting to eating flesh. He increased its ugliness by making it a corpse, since a carcass is repulsive. *Maytan* may be a state (ḥāl) of the brother or of his flesh. It has also been said that "you would hate it" is a statement about their condition after the affirmation (*taqrīr*). It is as if, when He had made them affirm, He said: "Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?" They answered: "We do not like that." Then He said to them: "You would hate it." After this there is an omitted clause, whose sense is: "So likewise, hate backbiting, which resembles it." This omission is indicated by the context. Upon this omitted clause is conjoined His saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said, and al-Rummani said: aversion to this flesh is called for by nature, while aversion to backbiting is called for by reason. Reason is more deserving of being answered, because it sees and knows, whereas nature is blind and ignorant. Al-Zamakhshari said: this verse contains many intensifiers. Among them is the interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; among them is the placing of what is most hateful in the sphere of love; among them is attributing the act to "one of you," and the indication that none of the two would like that; and among them is that He did not confine the image of backbiting to eating a human being's flesh but made it dead; and among them is that He did not confine the image of backbiting to eating a human being's flesh until He made him a brother to the one eaten.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 13:

﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾. Here "male" (dhakar) and "female" (unthā) refer to Adam and his wife. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is possible that it means the species, as if He said: 'Indeed We created each one of you from a male and a female.' But the first (interpretation) is more apparent and more sound, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: 'You are from Adam, and Adam is from dust.'" The purpose of the verse is the equality among people and the prohibition of what the Arabs used to do of boasting about lineages (aḥsāb) and disparaging ancestries (ansāb). So God made clear that nobility and honour before God are not by lineage and descent; rather, they are by piety (taqwā). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to be the most noble of people, let him fear God." It is also narrated that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded the Banū Bayāḍa to marry Abū Hind a woman from among them, but they said: "How shall we marry our daughters to our clients (mawālī)?"

﴿And We made you peoples (shuʿūb) and tribes (qabāʾil) that you may know one another﴾. Shuʿūb is the plural of shaʿb (with a fatḥah on the shīn), which is larger than the qabīla (tribe). Beneath it is the qabīla, then the baṭn (clan), then the fakhdh (sub-clan), then the faṣīla (immediate family), who are the nearest kin. Thus Muḍar, Rabīʿa and the like are shuʿūb, Quraysh is a qabīla, Banū ʿAbd Manāf is a baṭn, Banū Hāshim is a fakhdh, and it is said (the kh is) with a sukūn to distinguish it from the limb (jāriḥa). Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib is a faṣīla. It was said: the shuʿūb are among the non-Arabs (ʿajam), the qabāʾil among the Arabs, and the asbāṭ among the Children of Israel. The meaning of "li-taʿārafū" is that some of you may know one another.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 49, verse 14:**

﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed."﴾ It was revealed concerning the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, a tribe that lived near Madina. They displayed Islam, but they only loved spoils and the goods of this world. So Allah called them liars in their saying "we have believed," and He told the truth about them if they had said "we have submitted" (aslamna). This is based on the view that *iman* (faith) is affirmation by the heart, and *Islam* (submission) is submission expressed by the tongue through the two testimonies of faith, and by action through the limbs (*jawarih*). Thus *Islam* and *iman* are different in meaning in this context. They may also coincide, and *Islam* may be more general than *iman*, so that *iman* is included within it, as is stated in other passages.

﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you of anything of your deeds.﴾ The meaning of *lā yiltukum* is that He will not diminish anything of the rewards of your deeds. There are two forms of this word. It is said *lāta*, and this is the reading of Nafi'. It is also said *alta*, and this is the reading of Abu 'Amr, *lā ya'ltukum*, with a hamza before the lam.

If it is asked: how can He give them the rewards of their deeds when He has said that they have not believed, and that no deed is accepted except from a believer? The answer: obedience to Allah and His Messenger combines sincere faith and righteous deeds. The meaning is: if you return from what you are upon of faith with your tongues only and not with your hearts, and you perform righteous deeds, then Allah will not diminish anything of them for you.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 15:

﴿Then they did not doubt﴾ meaning: they did not have doubt about their faith. In this there is an implicit rebuke (ta'rid) of the Bedouins mentioned earlier, that they are in doubt. Likewise his saying about these people: ﴿It is they who are the truthful﴾ is also an implicit rebuke of the Bedouins, since they lied in their saying "We have believed." The reason ﴿then they did not doubt﴾ is joined with "then" (thumma) is to indicate the continuation of their faith over long and extended periods of time. ﴿And they strove﴾ means striving against the disbelievers, because it is evidence of the soundness of faith. It is unlikely that it means the striving against the self (nafs) and Satan (shaytan), given his saying: ﴿with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 49, verse 17:

﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have accepted Islam.﴾ It was revealed concerning the Banu Asad as well, for they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have believed in you and followed you, and we did not fight against you as Hawazin, Ghatafan and others did." ﴿Rather, Allah bestows favour upon you that He has guided you to faith.﴾ That is, He guided you to faith according to your claim. For this reason He said: ﴿if you are truthful.﴾ And "﴿bestows favour upon you﴾" may mean "bestows blessing upon you," or it may mean "mentions His blessing," and this latter is better because it corresponds to "they consider it a favour to you."
